utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Registrar, could you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon, everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case number IT-04-74-T, the Prosecutor versus Prlic et al. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Registrar. This is Tuesday, January 19, 2010, and I welcome our witness, first and foremost, then the accused, the counsel for Defence, and all members of the OTP in the courtroom, as well as everyone helping us. The Registrar has three IC numbers for us, I believe.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Some parties have submitted lists of documents to be tendered through Witness Vinko Maric. The list submitted by 4D shall be given Exhibit IC01157. The list submitted by the OTP has already been given Exhibit IC01158, and 4D and 2D have also submitted their objections to the Prosecution's list of documents tendered via Witness Vinko Maric. This list shall be given Exhibit IC01159 and 1160 respectively. The Prosecution has also submitted its objections to the lists of documents tendered by the Petkovic Defence team via Witness Vinko Maric. This list shall be given Exhibit IC01161. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Registrar. Let me now give the floor to Ms. Alaburic for the rest of her examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon to everyone in the courtroom. A very good afternoon to you, Mr. Jasak. Just to remind everyone, we started discussing Muslims as soldiers of the HVO yesterday. We said that there were Muslim soldiers in the units, that they were free to become members of the HVO, and there was no discrimination against them. I'll take it from there now.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jasak, when the first serious clashes broke out between the HVO and the BH Army, do you know what combat assignments Muslim soldiers of the HVO were primarily given?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The primary assignment was to defend from the VRS. They were deployed along the lines facing the VRS.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: How do you know that, given the fact that at the time you were already with the VOS of the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know because my former colleagues, whenever we met somewhere about town, having coffee together, or back at the Main Staff, would talk to me about it.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: At one point in 1993, did the Muslim soldiers of the HVO start leaving the HVO in considerable numbers?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. That was after the 9th of May.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: How did the HVO treat the Muslim soldiers who remained in the HVO after that?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The treatment that the Muslim soldiers in the HVO received after that was the same as everyone else. There was a great deal of appreciation for their decision to remain and to stick it out with their fellow fighters with whom they had been fighting the VRS from Day 1.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Let us now look at a number of documents now covering these topics. The first one up is P1083 -- P10180 [as interpreted] -- 180. Mr. Jasak, have you ever heard of this decision or, indeed, seen it?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I heard of it, and I saw it too.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: I want to know about paragraph 3 of this decision. The first section states that the HVO is made up by members of the Muslim and Croat peoples and other ethnicities, recognising the legal authorities of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina and pledging allegiance to them. If we look at this definition of multi-ethnicity as it applied to the HVO, would you say that that was the actual reality?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, if you look at this definition, you could say that that was how it worked out in practice too.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: If we move down to the next paragraph, it says that the Muslims were free to set up their own armed units, which would then be placed under the single command of the HVO, specifically the Mostar Municipal Staff. My first question: Did the Muslims in Mostar, in fact, set up their own units or forces?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they did. They set up an independent battalion in Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: How did that battalion evolve?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It grew and eventually ended up as a brigade, and the brigade was then transformed into the 4th Corps.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Are we talking about the BH Army?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right, we're talking about the BH Army, the 4th Corps of the BH Army.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jasak, this battalion that later became a brigade, was it really under the single command of the Mostar HVO?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was. The battalion, which later became a brigade, were under the single command of the Mostar HVO.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Did you hear about the HVO being subordinated, in an operative sense, to the BH Army Command in any local area across Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard that this was, in fact, the case in Sarajevo, Tuzla, and, I believe, Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Let's move on to the next document, 4D75. This is a letter written by the chief of the Main Staff, Milivoj Petkovic, and dispatched to Sefer Halilovic in February 1993. Mr. Jasak, I will read back to you a sentence from this document and ask you to please comment on it in your capacity as a former employee of the Main Staff at a time when Milivoj Petkovic was, in fact, chief of the Main Staff. So what we see happening here is Milivoj Petkovic telling his colleague, his counterpart in the BH Army, as follows, and I quote: "I was looking forward to every new fighter, be it a Croat or a Muslim, since I know that they shared an objective. The HVO has never changed its attitude towards the BH Army or its position regarding the BH Army. We are fully aware that neither the BH Army nor the HVO, as they are right now, can ever ultimately defeat the Chetniks." Mr. Jasak, what exactly would you say? What we see here in writing, was that a truthfully-expressed position by Milivoj Petkovic or was he actually trying to sell some lies to his counterpart in the BH Army, his colleague in the BH Army?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: He meant this truthfully. There was a long front-line facing the VRS or, rather, in the area that was liberated following fighting against the VRS. We needed men to actually man that line, and each new fighter was a welcome addition.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Did General Petkovic see the Muslim soldiers in the HVO as a factor of stability or as an element disrupting the stability of the HVO?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Petkovic --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I guess it didn't take too long. I raise the same question, the issues I raised yesterday as to foundation. What is the foundation of this evidence? Did this witness talk to Mr. Petkovic, did they talk? Did they go to church together and go to confession together and say, I really, really believe this to be true? I mean, what's the basis for expressing opinions about Mr. Petkovic's beliefs and feelings? There's no evidence in the record so far that provides any basis for this. Any witness can be asked this, essentially, which means that there's no basis for it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Alaburic, in order to prevent these kind of objections, which are a waste of time, as far as I'm concerned - I have more important things to do than listen to objections - please try to be more professional in the way you put your questions. You could have asked your witness, Did you meet Mr. Petkovic? Answer, Yes, No. If he says, Yes, go on. You can ask further ask him whether he talked with him. Answer, Yes. Then you can press on and say, Did you think the man had any qualities? And he says, Yes, and you can continue, and then the Prosecutor will not have to be on his feet and raise objections.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I believe that the objection by Mr. Scott was entirely unfounded. He was listening -- or, rather, had he been listening closely to my question, he would not have objected at all. In terms of your instructions to me to be professional, which would then probably mean that I'm being unprofessional, is just as unfounded. I think that sort of caution should have been addressed to Mr. Scott and not to me. If you look at the very beginning of my question about this, I said that I was asking Mr. Jasak this as a person who worked with General Petkovic back at the Main Staff. We have all seen his CV. We know that they spent time working together at the Main Staff; about eight months, in fact. I simply do not believe that I have to repeat that every single time I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Alaburic, you might know it, but the Prosecutor does not know it, obviously, and that is why he is raising to his feet. That's where the problem lies. Things are obvious for you, maybe, but you have four seconds to ask him to confirm what you know. You've worked with General Petkovic? Yes. And then you can go on. I'm not here to say he's wrong, he's right, or you're right, he's wrong. Absolutely not. We could do that, of course, but it will not be -- it's not what I'm going to have to decide on as far as the judgement is concerned. I'm going to have to decide on the individual liability of your client and not on Mr. Scott's objection. Sometimes they're justified, it's true, but sometimes I believe that it's just a waste of time. Maybe my colleagues don't feel like I do, but I do. I'm not saying you're not a professional, of course not, but I would rather that make sure that you prevent these kind of problems by putting your question in a different way. Establish a link between the witness and General Petkovic, and then when the connection is established, just further on, just press on, and we have no objection. Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: Sorry. Excuse me. I would like only to make a correction which is in this context, rather important, that in line 12 it is now written that when you spoke to Ms. Alaburic, that, I am not saying you are a professional, of course not. I believe that you wanted to say that, I am not saying that you are not a professional. But, therefore, I believe that it is a quite important difference, so this line should be corrected accordingly. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honours, it's --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for Mr. Scott, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: My apologies. Mr. President, Your Honours, I certainly don't -- it's certainly not my intention to try the Chamber's patience, and I wouldn't be on my feet unless I felt -- at least I felt professionally and in good faith that there was an objection that needed to be raised. To pick up on what you said, Mr. President, I don't think it's only what I don't know, and with the greatest respect, I don't think the Chamber can know, either, because of the basis of what's in the record so far. My colleagues and I last night, you know, read yesterday's testimony from top to bottom as to what this witness has told us so far since beginning his testimony yesterday about what he was doing at these various times, and, frankly, we know almost nothing. And Judge Trechsel at one point yesterday began to pick up on it. The witness went off on a bit of a tangent, gave, well, at best a partial answer, and then it went on from there. All we know is this man says he was in VOS, having something to do with the Main Staff, based somewhere in Mostar, between the period October 1992 and June 1993. In July and August 1993, he took on some other undefined responsibilities in Sector North, and in August of 1993 went to Zagreb. Now, I submit to Your Honours, unless I'm mistaken, which is always possible - I'm a human being, I am fallible - but my colleagues and I reviewed the testimony last night and that's all we know about this man. We don't know if he was sitting in a basement in Mostar with headsets on, listening to intercept communications. We don't know if he was Mr. Petkovic's aide-de-camp sitting at his elbow every day. We don't know if they ever talked during the war. To say that he worked for the Main Staff, a lot of people worked for the Main Staff in one respect or another, but may have never had a single conversation with Mr. Petkovic, may have never seen Mr. Petkovic. Now, that may be unlikely, but we don't know. And I think after at least one full day's testimony, with the greatest submission, and the reason I'm on my feet, is that there's still been no foundation by which we can judge the evidence of this witness. What is the point of spending two weeks listening to this witness if at the last -- two weeks from now we find out, Well, you know, I was sitting in my cubicle in the basement in West Mostar for three or four months writing reports, I never saw Mr. Petkovic, I was never out, I was never in Stolac, I was never here, I was never there. We don't know. It would be very simple, with the greatest respect to my colleague, who I have the great respect and affection for, it would be easy for her to tell us that.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, Your Honours, may I? May I say the following, please? I think we cannot do this with each and every witness who enters the courtroom, start with pre-history and then produce evidence to every single fact. We do believe that a number of facts have been sufficiently established so far. We are simply pressing on with our case. As for the cubicle in the basement and the unidentified location at which Mr. Jasak was working in Mostar, I do wish to draw your attention to one thing, and that is the evidence in this case, as follows: The ground plan of the building in Mostar where the Main Staff was actually based up until July 1993, room number 2 on that ground plan is clearly marked -- no, no, no, no, Your Honour, no. I am responding to Mr. Scott's objection. What I'm trying to say is this: Back then, we defined the exact location of the VOS. I can't be expected to go through this time and again with every single witness. I have the right to assume that Mr. Scott is familiar with the evidence as admitted. I'm at liberty to assume that Mr. Scott knows the exact location of the VOS. If he doesn't know that, if he's suspicious about anything at all, he will get a chance during his cross-examination to check this with the witness. There is one thing I'd like to check. I did establish a link with his ground plan, EC1146. I specifically asked the witness whether he had a chance to see it, to look at the ground plan. I asked him about the surface covered by this building. I asked him whether this was the building in which he, too, was working at the time, all of which he confirmed. I am pressing on. I am continuing with this story, assuming everyone now knows that the witness and his boss were sitting in that particular room of the Main Staff. Please, if I may be allowed to finish, Your Honours. I'm just trying to remind everyone that my question about this topic was on page 4, lines 22, 23, as follows: The witness, as an official of the Main Staff at the time that Milivoj Petkovic was there, should answer these questions, given his knowledge of General Petkovic, his acquaintance with General Petkovic. If this witness comes across something that he simply doesn't know, he will specify that. If Mr. Scott has any specific questions, he always has the cross-examination to try it out. Everything that Mr. Scott has been raising should have been raised on cross-examination and not now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Alaburic, you've talked at length, but you didn't say anything. Your case is the following: You're saying that you started from the ground plan that establishes where VOS was located, and then, I have my link, my connection. But it's not enough, and this is why Mr. Scott is right, because this person maybe was just, you know, cleaning the premises in the VOS or he was maybe just rank and file, and he was there, you know, placing the tapes so people could do the wire-tapping. I know he worked at the VOS, but what exactly was his job. This is what we need to know. This is what Mr. Scott asking you to find out, and you could have the answer in just two minutes. Just ask him: Did you supervise anyone, were you an officer? Answer, Yes. Did you meet Mr. Petkovic? Answer, Yes. Did you talk to Mr. Petkovic? Answer, Yes. And then you have your connection and your foundation, and then you could press on, because Mr. Scott is telling us, rightly so, that he has no idea who this man -- what this man was doing. It's a question that he has, and everyone could have the same question in mind. But it only takes a few questions to get the answer, and you don't have to use the document of the ground plan, this ground plan, because that's not sufficient as far as I'm concerned. He could have been just, you know, the cleaning person in that building. We need to know exactly what his job was. Put a few questions and solve the problem and find the connection, and that way we will prevent objections. That's the way to do the job.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I would like to remind you that we covered this witness's CV. It was stated, with perfect clarity, that the witness first worked as a battalion commander and then came to the VOS at the Main Staff. He was an analyst, and he was in charge of the Eastern Herzegovina Operation Zone. Therefore, there is no doubt as to whether he was a cleaner at the building or not. His position is perfectly clear. The answers were addressed regarding certain documents. I went through that time and again, and I simply fail to understand how there could be anyone in this courtroom who still doesn't get it. As for the ground plan in the building and mentioning that, Your Honour, Judge Antonetti, I would like to say the following: That was my response to Mr. Scott's objection, when he said that the witness may as well have been working in a cubicle somewhere in the basement. I have to say that I find an objection or remark like that as entirely unfounded and perhaps not sufficiently serious. I regret that you fail to protect me this time around, as the Prosecutor is normally protected from any objections raised by one of the Defence teams. I do believe that we now can press --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Alaburic, I'm protecting no one. I'm not here to protect anyone, the Prosecutor or anyone. All I want is the job to be done professionally so that there are no objections, because what's interesting for myself, as a Judge, and for the entire Bench, I believe, is to take a look at the documents and see what is written in the documents. That's the important thing. And if he knows what's in the document, we need to know why it is that he knows what is in this document. Did he see documents written by Mr. Petkovic at the time? Did he see any political analysis drafted by Mr. Petkovic at the time? That is what we are interested in, that's all. Now, you can use your time as you want, and if Mr. Scott raises to his feet, fine, he will.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, Your Honour, I believe that my learned friend Mr. Scott has every right to object, which doesn't solely mean that each and every objection he raises is well founded. I don't know what his objection will be about. He decided to do that, and that's why he is in this courtroom. After so many months, I have no idea why, just to be perfectly open and sincere about that. As far as any further examination that I may or may not have on this document, you haven't given me a chance to ask my questions. I started to ask my first question about that, and then Mr. Scott objected, and then now we spend the rest of the time talking about that. Had you allowed meet to begin with to complete my examination based on that particular document and had there been anything relevant that remained to be clarified, I would have been entirely in agreement with this statement. Nevertheless, I was never given a chance to start examining the witness on this document, and I realise now that my learned friend Mr. Karnavas has something to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If I may be of some assistance in this instance. I think perhaps some foundation was laid, but not the entire foundation which would be satisfying Mr. Scott. I think what needs to be done is for the next 10 or 15 minutes, go back a little bit and then ask certain details that would then allow the linkage that you are saying -- that you are suggesting, Judge Antonetti. I think Mr. Scott would be satisfied with that. I think that's what's missing here. So rather than spending the next 15 or 20 minutes discussing this, I think a series of 5 or 10 questions, as far as the detailing of exactly the gentleman's work, what exactly he did, when, where, how, and with whom, that might be of assistance and then we can move on, and I'm sure that Mr. Scott would not be objecting, because these are fundamental issues to the foundation which, in all due fairness to him, he's entitled to make these sort of objections, although under all the circumstances, you know, they may not be warranted. So, in any event, I just want to make sure that we can go forward, because we're just wasting time, and some of us are sitting here just wondering where are we going with this.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jasak, what exactly were you doing during your time with the VOS?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was an adviser to the chief of the Military Intelligence Service, the VOS, at the HVO Main Staff. My work was normally assigned to me by the chief of service. I analysed the situation in South-Eastern Herzegovina and, more specifically, in Mostar, for the most part.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: I'm spending my time asking you about these questions. What exactly do you mean when you say that you were into analysis work, that you worked as an analyst?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: What that means is that any reports coming from the field that had to do with this area that I specified were analysed by me. I would then draw up a section of the report that was later dispatched by the Military Intelligence Service to the recipients that I mentioned before; chief of the Defence Department, chief of the Main Staff, president of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, and possibly other addressees as well whenever necessary.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Based on these reports from the ground, would you envisage what the BH Army might do next?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell us, were you able, based on certain information you received, to gain an overview of an event and to predict further developments?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell us, were the reports made by you and your service the basis on which the commander of the Main Staff made decisions?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course they were.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Based on your reports, did the chief and later the command of the Main Staff draw up his reports, for example, on work or on a current situation?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is the part relating to enemy activities.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Did you know General Petkovic personally?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did know General Petkovic from the time before I joined the Main Staff. Since early October to mid-July, I collaborated with General Petkovic in the Main Staff. We worked together.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Were you able to form an opinion as to what sort of man he was, what his priorities were, what he wanted to happen in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Petkovic's priority was to defend the area from the Army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: I didn't ask you that, but I asked you whether you were able to get to know him as a man and as an officer.

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely, yes. When you are working together in such a small area, such a small space, and the entire Main Staff numbered some 15 people, of course we all knew each other well.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Is that the source of your knowledge about General Petkovic, on the basis of which you responded to the question about the document we just saw?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the basis was my personal contacts with General Petkovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jasak, let's look at the next document, 2D150. This is a document issued by the Personnel Department of the Defence Department. The date is June 1993. That's very important. Let's look at the summary information about the national breakdown of members of the HVO. At that time, according to this document, there were 16.19 per cent Muslims in the HVO. In the 1st Brigade, there were 35 per cent Muslims, in the 2nd Brigade 20, in the 3rd Brigade 13.6. In view of the fact that this was an operative zone you were in charge of in the VOS, telling us, according to your information, is this information here correct?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this information is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Excuse me, Ms. Alaburic. Witness, I would like to insist again on foundation, because your task was to gather information about the enemy, not about the HVO, was it? Did you have a double function? Did you also gather information about what went on within the HVO, what the mood was, what the relation between Muslims and Croats within the HVO was, and so forth?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the information listed here for the 1st, 2nd, 3rd, and 4th Brigade of the South-East Herzegovina Operative Zone was common knowledge. You can see here that this document was dated the 9th of June. In the 3rd Brigade, for example, it says "201 men." Before that, there were many more men. But after the 9th of May, two battalions left this brigade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: You say this is common knowledge. Here, we have very detailed figures with two figures after the comma in percentage. Can I take your answer as meaning that you roughly know this, as common knowledge?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't be precise up to two decimal points, but more or less those were the figures.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, my next question would have been, How do you know this? But the witness has just said that.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: You said that the number of Muslims in the 3rd Brigade was much larger before the 9th of May. What can you tell us about the 2nd Brigade?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: This number is correct. A smaller number left the 2nd Brigade than the number that left the 3rd Brigade, so that most of the Muslims in the 2nd Brigade stayed there.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jasak, did the VOS and the SIS co-operate?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for the co-operation between the VOS and the SIS, all I know is that the chiefs collaborated at their level. But I, myself, did not collaborate with anyone at mine.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: I was asking you about the institutional level. Did VOS co-operate with the Department of the Interior and the civilian Secret Service?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the highest levels, all the security and intelligence services co-operated and exchanged information.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: When you say that they exchanged information, does that mean that you, in the VOS, had information which you did not receive directly from the ground, but you received them from other security and intelligence services?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Exchange of information means that if one service finds out something belonging to the purview of another, that information should be forwarded to that service. So we would get that sort of information from the other services.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: His Honour Judge Trechsel asked you if you, in the VOS, dealt with the enemy. How did it come about that you had information concerning internal matters within the HVO? You said that these things were common knowledge, but my question now is: Did VOS have official information about this coming from other institutions in Herceg-Bosna?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that was possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I find that not quite precise. You say "it was possible." Are you saying that VOS had knowledge of this list here or do you just say it may be that it had knowledge of this list?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I said "maybe," but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you. That's all I wanted to be sure about. And the second point. You have talked about the exchange of information, and you have said that one service, let's say SIS, would inform another service, let's say VOS, if it gained information that was important for VOS. Now, this is an internal matter -- information, so according to what you have told us just now, this is not something that SIS would share with VOS because it was not something that entered the realm of activity of VOS? Have I understood this correctly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is not a SIS document, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: That is -- I wasn't actually saying that. But it could be, could it not? Let's say, SIS would, for instance, say that in the 108th Brigade there are tensions between Muslims and Croats. That is an information they would not forward to VOS, if I have understood you correctly.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I don't know what SIS would do in a situation of that sort.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I leave it at that.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jasak, if a certain number of soldiers of Muslim ethnicity left the HVO and joined the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, does the fact of strengthening the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina have any meaning for you in VOS?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: The fact of transferring to the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, does this information become relevant as information on a possibly hostile army?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The information becomes relevant.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: In the Main Staff, was there ever a meeting which you attended or which was attended by your chief and then he passed the information on to you? Was there ever any discussion at any such meeting about the departure of large numbers of Muslims from the HVO?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, at the level of our service, there was talk about the large numbers of Muslims going over to the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: I will now show you two witness statements, and I will ask you to comment on them.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: (redacted). To the best of your knowledge, Stolac is the area of the 1st Brigade. Was there really a significant percentage of Muslim soldiers in that brigade?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there certainly was a significant number of Muslim soldiers there.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Another witness, CJ, said that he didn't know of a single example of discrimination against Muslims in the HVO in April or May 1993. That's on page 10952. Tell us, Mr. Jasak, if you know whether, according to your knowledge, there were any examples of discrimination against Muslims in the HVO in the operative zone you analysed.

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had no such information or, rather, no information indicating that there was any sort of discrimination.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Let's look at some documents now. 4D16 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, let's stay with this document. I know that your field of specialty at the time was to conduct analysis from documents about the BiH, and hence the question by my colleague as to whether you knew anything about the JV [as interpreted]. I have the same question. I have a Congolese Judge, a Swiss Judge, and a fourth Judge, and I know how the other Chambers are made of. For that reason, from the document which I have here, there's one thing which I find surprising, and maybe you can help me here. Look at 36, the battalion of -- Convicts Battalion. That's at the very end of the document. Had you heard about the Convicts Battalion? I'm going to try and lay the foundation.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I have heard about the Convicts Battalion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you are aware of that, so there will be no objections about that. Okay. So this document states there are 280 of them: Croats, 164; Muslims, 116, almost 41.42 per cent. I'm just finding out that the Convicts Battalion that we talk a lot about here in this trial is almost, for half of it, made up of Muslims. Some state that the Convicts Battalion was directly connected to Mate Boban in a specific chain of command. If this assumption is true -- I don't know about that, we'll see about that at the end of the trial, but if it is true, that would mean that Mate Boban had at his disposal a striking power made up of 50 per cent of Muslims, a striking power that he would have used in military operations against Muslims, particularly in Sovici-Doljani. So according to you, from a military standpoint, how do you analyse that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, this question is a little bit too broad. As for the percentage here, I did not have any direct contact with that unit. I did have direct contact with the units in the South-East Herzegovina Operative Zone. I knew some commanders who had been in the Convicts Battalion; for example, Zijo Orucevic , who later went over to the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. I knew there were Muslims, but I am now speaking about the men I knew who were in units in the South-East Herzegovina Operative Zone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is dated 9th of June. It comes from the Department of Defence, Office of the Human Resource Administration. 6th of June. No, sorry, 9th of June, sorry about that. So before the 30th of June, so before Muslims started leaving the HVO. As far as you know -- and if you don't know, tell us so. As far as you know, after the 30th of June, did Muslims leave the Convicts Battalion in order to join the BiH Army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I don't know how many Muslims from the Convicts Battalion went over to the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, but here number 36 on page 1 -- well, it doesn't say that, it doesn't contain the information for this unit, so I don't know what the situation was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. So you don't know exactly what the situation was. Thank you very much. You've answered my question. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I would like to stay another moment with this table. It lists also high-level units, perhaps within quotes: The Department of Defence, 3.6 per cent; Main Staff, 1.5 per cent; Posavina Command, 15; JIH Command, 8.88; Command of Central Bosnia, 1.12; Command of the Operation Zone SZH, 0.00. Now, you have affirmed that there was no discrimination against Muslims. It is -- however, it appears that in the higher units, Muslims are in very small number, much smaller than on the top level. Wouldn't that sort of suggest that perhaps in the area of promotions and calling for higher command, Croats are clearly preferred in comparison to Muslims?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, to the best of my knowledge, I have no knowledge of any kind of discrimination. Promotions depended on ability shown on the ground.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Prosecutor, you were standing up.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. President, Your Honours. I just want to make a point for the record, Your Honour. On transcript page 20, from line 17, there was a reference to a pseudonym witness. It's the first pseudonym witness that was referred to, and in the transcript reference, and I just need to point out that these pages were in private session, Your Honour, with this testimony, so that may require redaction. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, could you please look into it with the Legal Officer. You may proceed, Ms. Alaburic.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jasak, let's look at 4D1633. As we can see, this is issued by the commander of the 2nd Brigade on the 16th of July, 1993, and it's his approval for the de-mobilisation of a soldier. Judging by his name, this was a Muslim, and he was being de-mobilised at his own request. It says that he returned the equipment he had been issued with and his military identity card and weapons. Did you know anything about the procedure for demobilisation, sir?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Does this document show in what way a soldier was de-mobilised on personal request?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Regardless of the name of the soldier, this document shows the procedure whereby any soldier of the HVO might be demobilised.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: The brigade in question here is the 2nd Brigade, Mr. Jasak. Did you know that a certain number of soldiers of Muslim ethnicity left the 2nd Brigade and asked to be demobilised?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did know there were such requests after the 9th of May.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: The next document is 4D1223. It was issued by the commander of the 2nd Brigade of the HVO. It's dated the 18th of June, 1993. It's a proposal for demobilisation of 25 soldiers. Judging by their names, they were Muslims. And the reason is: Failure to turn up in their unit from the 9th of May, 1993. Mr. Jasak, did know that some soldiers of Muslim ethnicity simply failed to show up in their units after the 9th of May?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did know of that. Such soldiers were then demobilised, so they were no longer members of those units.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: From this document, it follows that the brigade commander submitted the proposal for demobilisation. Was this the rule?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The rule was that commanders of battalions should submit their proposals to the brigade commander, and the brigade commander would forward these to the South-East Herzegovina Operative Zone.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Let's look at the next document, 4D1224. Again, it's issued by the commander of the 2nd Brigade, and he's proposing the demobilisation of 41 soldiers because they had not turned up in their units from the 9th of May, 1993, onwards. So does this show the same situation we've just been talking about?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this document confirms what we just said. This is another battalion of the same brigade.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: You told us that the brigade commander forwarded the proposals to the command of the operative zone. Judging by the stamp here, to whom was this proposal sent?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It says that this was received in the Operations Zone of South-East Herzegovina on the 18th of June, 1993, on the same day it was written.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: So it was forwarded in the manner you described?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: The next document is 4D1639. And this is consent from the commander of the 2nd Brigade for the demobilisation of soldiers, at their personal request. Judging by the name of the soldier, he was a Muslim. The consent was issued on the 22nd of June, 1993. Mr. Jasak, did you know that in June, in the Operations Zone of South-East Herzegovina, Muslim soldiers were leaving their units following the proper procedure and being demobilised?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did have such information.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: From the stamp showing receipt of the documents, it follows that this was forwarded to the Operations Zone of South-East Herzegovina. Is that the proper procedure, to the best of your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, that was precisely the proper procedure.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Another document about this, 4D1634, the 2nd Brigade commander's consent to demobilise for personal reasons. Judging by the name, this soldier was an ethnic Muslim. Tell us, please, who this consent was addressed to.

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: This consent by the brigade commander was sent to the Eastern Herzegovina Operations Zone.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: If we look at the left-hand bottom side of the document, who this was addressed to, the section for structure and personnel, was this the section that was then supposed to complete the demobilisation procedure?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was down to them, and they were supposed to work with the defence office on this.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jasak, when you were with the HVO, which country did you believe you were defending?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: As a soldier of the HVO, I believed I was defending Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Did you believe yourself to be a member of the armed forces of Bosnia-Herzegovina as a country, as a state?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Most certainly.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: P274 is our next document. This is a decision by the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina to declare a state of war. Mr. Jasak, did you have any information indicating that the BH Presidency had declared a state of war in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I knew that.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Let us have a look together at how they define the aggressor. Based on paragraph 1 of this decision, who appears to be the aggressor, or the enemy, if you like?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: An act of aggression was carried out by the Republic of Serbia-Montenegro, the Yugoslav Army, and the terrorist of the Serbian Democratic Party.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Can you look at the second-to-last bullet, please, saying that the aggressor has occupied over 70 per cent of the territory of the state of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and the aggressor is refusing to halt their aggression. I want to know about how this 70 per cent breaks down. Mr. Jasak, if the aggressor, indeed, occupied 70 per cent of the territory, how much of the BH territory remained free?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: 30 per cent.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: This decision was issued on the 20th of June, 1992. At the time, was part of the BH territory under the control of the HVO Army?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right, a considerable portion of the free territory was HVO controlled. We are looking at 30 per cent free territory. The HVO was holding about 70 per cent of that territory, meaning about 21 per cent of the overall BH territory.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jasak, let's assume you're an analyst working with an intelligence service. If you were to analyse this document in that official capacity, what could you tell us? What is the position of the BH Presidency concerning the territory being held by the HVO? Is that considered to be occupied territory or free territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Beyond a shadow of a doubt, it is considered free territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Next document, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, there are two important questions that I must put to you from this document. Now, to lay the foundation, I will put a very simple question to you. First, you know how to read? Can you read? I know it sounds stupid, but it's important.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, you can read. When you read something, do you understand what you read?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. You understand what you read. Now, take a look at number 2. It says: "The proclamation of the state of war aims at, based on the individual and collective right of citizens to self-defence..." This is written black and white. This is written by Mr. Izetbegovic on June 20th, 1992. Let's mentally go back to the region of Sarajevo at the time. We know that the BH Army is not yet set up as an army, so when saying this, does this mean that Mr. Izetbegovic is asking all citizens, whoever they may be, to defend themselves, either individually or collectively? Is this what this sentence means?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, yes, that's what it says, and this applies to all citizens.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. As far as you're concerned now, could you tell us that this is why Croat citizens believed that it was their duty to join the HVO, just like Muslim citizens believed that it was also their duty to join the HVO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, that's right. Each citizen who wished to defend against the aggressor joined the HVO. The HVO was established before the 20th of June, 1992. It was, in fact, established in April of that year.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Please read number 3 in your own language. Could you tell us what is written under number 3? Could you please read it out loud so that the interpreters can interpret what you are saying?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "The armed forces of Bosnia and Herzegovina are hereby authorised to take necessary measures to organise a general national resistance in order to reach such goals as have been set."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I asked you to read this out loud in your own language for a simple reason, because I see that there is a plural being used, "the armed forces," plural. It's not "the Army of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina." What is written here is "the armed forces," plural. Why is there a plural? Could you tell us what this plural means, as far as you're concerned?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, what that means to me is the BH Army and the HVO.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: If I may. Witness, what is the singular of "the armed forces"? If there is just one army in a country, how are they called?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "Oruzana snaga" or a particular army would simply be named.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Excuse me. I should not have asked you the question, because it's a linguistic one. I think that in English, "the armed forces" are the army. The army is referred to as "armed forces" because usually it has terrestrial and others, but I stand to be corrected.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, I, with respect, I believe I would correct you, Your Honour. "The armed forces" we would understand to be the army, the navy, the air force. The air force is a force. Certainly, I -- that's what I've -- I've never been in any of them, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: That's exactly what I was saying.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: That's exactly what I was saying. But it does not -- "armed forces" does not mean that they are really entities under a different top head.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I'm not an expert. I'm just a true-born Englishman.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Okay. I think I -- best to drop this altogether. Mr. Prlic, as a linguistic expert in English --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRLIC
utterances.text: This is simply grammatic. And on the part which Judge Prandler [sic] started, if you compare translation from Croatian to English, in Croatian language word "armed forces" is written with not capital letters, it was written with small letters, which means that it is not just one armed force. If you look at the English version, a sentence started "The armed forces," and I think this is the reason why Judge Trechsel, if I may say, put this question, because this is absolutely plural. "Armed forces" in Croat language, it is not capital. If it is capital letter, it means that this is going to be one army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you very much. That is -- I think when you first spoke of Judge Prandler, perhaps you also meant me, whose name is Trechsel, as you know.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRLIC
utterances.text: Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: That's okay. I think it was really a linguistic intermezzo, and I don't think there are any consequences to be drawn from this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kovacic, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm afraid that we have another linguistic problem there. The interpretation at page 30, line 3. Paragraph 3, as interpreted, and the witness read it out carefully, the original, and I'll re-read this, runs as follows: "The armed forces of Bosnia and Herzegovina are hereby authorised to take necessary measures ..." This verb, "prevzeti," that's how the Croatian reads, which has been translated as "to take necessary measures," and that wouldn't quite be it, because "prevzeti" means take over from someone; in other words, something already exists and that is now meant to be taken over by someone else. Nevertheless, I can't be categorical about this. That's why I called it a linguistic problem to begin with. Are we talking about Serbian or Croatian? In Serbian, it could possibly mean this, but at any rate, this term, "prevzeti" in my opinion implies that they are supposed to take over something, take over an existing defence or something, but not necessarily, as I said. This is a problem that we have with Serbian as opposed to Croatian.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Colonel, let's not spend too much time on these linguistic problems, but I believe there are two interpretations: Either the force armies are made up of the BH Army and the HVO, which is what you told us, or they are made up of the navy, the air force, and land forces, the army. Now, at the time in June 1992, the Republic of -- could you tell us whether the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina had a navy and an air force? Did they?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, they had maybe one or two helicopters but nothing that you could refer to as an air force. And the same applied to the HVO, they were land forces, for the most part. The BH Army and the HVO, the two components of the Armed Forces of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Ms. Alaburic.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The next document, P339, the agreement on friendship and co-operation. On the 1st [as interpreted] of July, 1992, the agreement was signed by Franjo Tudjman and Alija Izetbegovic in Zagreb. Could we please focus on paragraph 6 of this agreement. I quote: "The armed component of the HVO is an integral component of the armed forces of Bosnia and Herzegovina." Let's stop right there. They say that I should correct the date. The 21st of July, and not the 1st of July, as recorded.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jasak, since we have now assured ourselves that you can read, you're able to read this, you worked as an analyst, what is your interpretation of this sentence? What is the relationship between the HVO and the BH Army?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: This clearly shows that the armed component of the HVO is a component of the joint armed forces of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, on an equal footing with the BH Army.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: What was your personal view at the time in mid-1992, say, on this subject?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The same as here, the way it's written here. The HVO was a component of the armed forces of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jasak, do you have any information indicating that anyone at any point in time tried to abolish the HVO Army?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I have no information indicating anything like that.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Next document, please, P476, a decision by the Constitutional Court of Bosnia-Herzegovina. The date is the 14th of September, 1992. Mr. Jasak, I will not be asking you any legal questions about this document. Nevertheless, please have a look. There is a total of nine paragraphs contained in this decision, and a number of legal documents are abolished or declared null and void. Does the list include the decision to establish the HVO?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that is not one of the documents that were quashed by the Constitutional Court of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Next document, P151. Can you tell us what this document is about, Mr. Jasak?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's this is a decision to establish the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Was the army known as the HVO, in fact, established based on this decision?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Do you have any knowledge indicating that anyone at any time overturned, abolished, or declared this decision null and void?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no knowledge of that at all.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Next document, 4D410, a decree on the Armed Forces of Bosnia-Herzegovina -- on the Armed Forces of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. We have here a copy that was published in the "Official Gazette" of the BH Army. Paragraph or Article 1 reads: "The republic's armed forces shall comprise the Croatian Defence Council." Mr. Jasak, would this document seem to confirm or deny that the HVO was, indeed, a component of the Armed Forces of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: This document clearly confirms that the HVO was a component of the Armed Forces of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Next document, 4D --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, earlier I asked you a question on the plural, and we had a debate on -- a semantic debate on -- between some of us in this courtroom, but I didn't have this decree at hand. This is a decree written by Mr. Izetbegovic, himself. It's not a decree written by the HVO. This was written by the president of the Presidency of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina on August 6th, 1992. In Article 1, we see that there is a plural used again, and we see that there is mention of the BH Army and the HVO. What's your take on this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's right, Your Honour. Bosnia and Herzegovina has two armies, the armed forces, as it reads, comprising two components, the BH Army and the HVO.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I know you're not a legal expert and you were an analyst within the VOS, which is why I asked you if you can read, write, and understand a sentence. Anyone, you know, with a high school degree, and I'm not talking about a faculty professor or anything, but anyone who can read and write, when they see that it's written, black and white, that the HVO is part of the Armed Forces of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, does this mean that there are two components to the army; the BH Army, on the one hand, and the HVO, on the other hand? I mean, I believe any child could answer this question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's right, Your Honour, two components of the Armed Forces of Bosnia and Herzegovina, one being the BH Army, the other being the HVO.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Would you agree with me to note that this document was not written by the HVO, but by Mr. Izetbegovic, himself?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, this document was signed by the president of the Presidency of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, Alija Izetbegovic, not the HVO.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fair enough.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Witness, still on this document and this fact, were there one or two commands of the two armies? You've said there were two armies. Did each army have its own command; do you know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I do know that. Each of the armies had its own command. Nevertheless, there was an attempt -- a lasting attempt throughout to create a single command.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: If you look at the decree, Article 1, there is a part then that is in inverted commas. And in the second part, does it not say that the HVO places themselves, both parties -- both parts of the army place themselves under the single command of the army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, which portion of the document are you referring to exactly; Article 1?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Yes, as I have indicated, Article 1, which has two parts, one which is a small three-line text without quotation marks, and then there come quotation marks, and then there are three subparagraphs, and I'm talking about the second one.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, it says here "the army." Nevertheless, if you look at the title, itself, "Decree Law on Amendments to the Decree Law on the Armed Forces of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina," I see the HVO - and that was the case years ago as well - as a component of the Armed Forces of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: But I asked you a different question. I asked you about the single command. Did you see that, that there should be a single command, and who has the single command?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the single command was supposed to comprise the BH Army and the HVO. Nevertheless, at the time this was produced, both components were still being organised. Attempts had been made earlier to set up a single command at the highest level.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Please proceed, Ms. Alaburic.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour Judge Trechsel, if I may, we shall be dealing with this at quite some length in our briefs. We believe that this is a question of legal interpretation. This section, the sentence saying "being placed under the single command of the army," it's about the position of the comma in that sentence, and the question is whether that applies to other armed units, too, in additional to the HVO, but we'll be shedding more light on that matter further down the road. The next document is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm sure you will, Ms. Alaburic, but I have not taken this document before this witness, who apparently has a bit difficulties in reading a legal document, so you will definitely discuss this at length. I'm interested and looking forward to reading you.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour Judge Trechsel, if I may explain one thing which I believe is very important. I asked this witness questions about this document in much the same way as Judge Antonetti phrased his question. This witness holds a degree in engineering. I'm not expecting from this witness any sophisticated legal interpretations in terms of whether a comma should be there or elsewhere, in terms of whether a particular section or a particular sentence refers to the HVO or someone else as well. All I wish to raise with this witness is issues regarding the relationship between the HVO and the BH Army within the Armed Forces of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. The next document is 4D1524.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I think we'll probably have a break. I just want to say no need to explain or justify. It's perfectly all right, what you did. I was just trying to explain why I went into this and that I did not have the idea to take up such questions with this witness originally. But I think probably it's time for the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, it's almost 10 to 4.00. We're going to take a 20-minute break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Alaburic, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: The next document, Mr. Jasak, is 4D1524. This is a letter containing information sent by Sefer Halilovic to the Main HVO Staff in Grudica [as interpreted] on the 8th of August, 1992. In item 1, I'm interested in only the following part. It says that something is not favourable to the Army of Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, which also comprises the armed formations of the HVO, and it's not to the advantage of the Croatian people either. So how would you comment on this, Witness?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: This can only be interpreted as follows: The armed formations of the HVO are an integral part of the Armed Forces of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Let's look at the next document, 1D14 -- 2432.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction, 2432.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: This is an order issued by the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina, signed by President Alija Izetbegovic on the 16th of October, 1992. Item 1 reads as follows: "The Armed Forces of Bosnia-Herzegovina (the Army of BH and the HVO) ..." Tell us, Mr. Jasak, had this document reached your intelligence service, what would you have said? What was the standpoint of the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina in October 1992 as to the component parts of the Armed Forces of BH?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this is common knowledge. The Armed Forces of Bosnia-Herzegovina had two components, the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina and the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: The next document, 2D1470. 2D470, correction. This is an agreement reached in Zenica on the 20th of April, 1993, by Sefer Halilovic and Milivoj Petkovic, who signed the document. In item 1 of this document, it says: "The BH Army and the HVO are legal military forces of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and are treated equally." Had this document reached your intelligence service, what would you have said about the equality of the Army of BH and the HVO in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It clearly follows from this document that the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina and the HVO are legal military forces of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, that they are treated equally, that they have the same rights and the same obligations.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honours, but I was hoping we were moving on to something else, but I'll have to go back to where we were before. What additional value is this witness adding to the document? There's been periods in the case where we've simply had the document -- the witness reading documents. I think we can all agree that if I read the words on the page, that is what they say, and we can all read that and it says whatever it says. But what additional value has this -- evidentiary value has this witness added to that, other than to say that's what the document says? Before the break, there was a number of interventions and comments by both the Judges and others that the man's not a lawyer. He might have been an analyst. I don't recall him being qualified as a constitutional lawyer. In fact, I don't recall him being qualified as an expert on anything. Your Honour, let me make the Prosecution point abundantly transparent, if it's not already. There's two fundamental problems with this witness. One, he's been brought to address a number of things that he has no foundation to address. He was a lower-level analyst at the time, and yet they want to make him an all-purpose -- know-everything witness, number 1, without foundation, number 1. Number 2, they want to use him as an expert. We didn't get an expert report. There is nothing -- he's not being tendered to qualify as an expert, and yet they want him to address -- now we're talking about an expert on legal matters. He just said, Undoubtedly shows it's a legal organisation, a legal part of the armed forces. That is purely and simply a legal conclusion. It cannot be characterised any other way. Now, that's the problem with this witness. He's being addressed, talked about, asked about things he has no foundation to address, and they want to use him as an expert without complying with the rules on an expert. If they want to make him an expert under Rule 94, they could have tendered him as such, they could have given us a report just as Mr. Tomljanovich and others, and we could have treated him as an expert, but they haven't done that. And those are two of the fundamental problems with this witness and why the Prosecution, in this instance -- why I have been on my feet so much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Alaburic, do you still want to answer to this? If not, I'd like to ask the witness a question.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I think there's no need to respond to the objection raised by my learned friend Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, we have looked at a number of documents from various sources, BH Army, the HVO, Alija Izetbegovic, including the international community, and including the international community that was shown in the last document. As we read the documents, if you're a reasonable Judge, you may reach the conclusion that there were two armies, HVO and the BH Army, that there could be one single command, and that these two armies, as is stated in the last document signed by the international community, by its two high representatives, recognised that these two armies were to be treated on an equal footing, treated equally. So you've heard the Prosecutor, but it's the Prosecutor who intervened. What's the connection between you and these documents? According to you, were you in a legal army or were you in an army which was illegal? That's the basic question, really, that I'm asking you. What's your answer on this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I was a member of a legal army which was one of the components of the Armed Forces of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and that was the HVO.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. You heard the Prosecutor. He said you're not a legal expert, you're not a lawyer. How can you say that you were in a legal army, I mean, from your point of view?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] An army fighting for Bosnia-Herzegovina, as a whole, against an aggressor can only be legal. It cannot be anything else. That was the basis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So if I understand you correctly, you had the strong conviction that you belonged to an army from the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, or did you belong to an army of this entity, Herceg-Bosna, the HVO community -- the Croat Defence Community, the Republic of Herceg-Bosna? I mean, what was the entity which was in your -- for which there was -- referring to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I belonged -- Your Honour, I belonged to the HVO, which was fighting for a united, unitary Bosnia-Herzegovina, so it was part of the Armed Forces of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, thank you for your question. You really realised what I was getting at. I just want to correct the transcript to avoid problems.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: When you say you were fighting for Bosnia-Herzegovina, tell us, what sort of Bosnia-Herzegovina were you fighting for? What did you say?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: For Bosnia-Herzegovina, a republic which is unitary, which is whole, which is the republic of all its citizens. So we were fighting only against the aggressor.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not a legal expert. I'm afraid the word "unitary" might refer to unitarism. Is it all right? No, my colleague is saying the interpretation is not good, that it's not good to say "unitary" for the word "jedinstven." "Jedinstven" should mean territorial [realtime transcript read in error "military"] integrity, because unitarism is an issue of internal organisation. The witness did not say he was fighting for a unitary Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Now it says that "Jedinstven."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for Judge Trechsel, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: "Jedinstven" should mean military unity, but you said "territorial unity," I think.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's wrongly recorded. I did not say "military unity." I said "territorial integrity." "Territorially," single, means territorial integrity.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A whole Bosnia-Herzegovina, within its borders, the borders of AVNOJ.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We now have a problem, because part of the witness's answer is recorded as if I was the speaker.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Could you please repeat what you said, Witness?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Bosnia-Herzegovina, in its entirety within the borders of AVNOJ.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I think now it's precise. Your Honour Judge Antonetti, thank you for your questions about this document. My intention was to establish the mens rea, which is why I am using this document. Document P2078, 2078. This is a joint statement which, on the 25th of April, 1993, was signed in Zagreb by Mate Boban and Alija Izetbegovic, and co-signed by Dr. Franjo Tudjman.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jasak, let us try to analyse not as lawyers, but as you would have analysed this document in the Intelligence Service. It says: "The co-signatories of this statement call upon all the members of the armed forces to respect all the agreements reached to date between the representatives of the Muslim and Croatian people in the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina." And they now refer to the previous order, and we can see that from the content of the agreement in Zenica in April 1993. My question, Mr. Jasak, is as follows: Who signed these military [as interpreted] agreements as the representative of the Croatian people?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The representative of the Croatian people who signed this agreement was Mate Boban.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do apologise, but again we have an error in the transcript. Page 45, line 9, I think my colleague did not say "military agreements," she just spoke about agreements.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Correct, I spoke about agreements, and I said -- so I was referring to all the agreements signed up to that point, all the previous agreements. And when referring to the agreement --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Ms. Alaburic, I don't think that's proper. "All the previous agreements"? Which agreements? Was the witness shown these agreements, is he aware of them? I find this really too vague, "all previous agreements ."

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, please look at the next sentence. I really don't have time to read every sentence from all these old documents. I've been through all these sentences with the witness. But if you look at the continuation of the sentence, you can see that the Army of BH and the HVO are equally legal units. And if we recall the previous document we looked at, or, rather, a document we looked at previously, and that's 2D470, a careful analyst, looking at the legal and intelligence aspects of this, there's no problem in referring to this agreement as well as all previous agreements. What I'm interested in right now is defining all these agreements as agreements between the Croatian and Muslim peoples.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: So the previous agreement, the one from Zenica, was signed by Petkovic and Halilovic? Who signed on behalf of the Croatian people?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Milivoj Petkovic, the chief of the Main Staff of the HVO, signed on behalf of the Croatian people.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: And who is the signatory on behalf of the Muslim people?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
