utterances.text: On behalf of the Muslim people, the signatory is the chief of the Staff of the Supreme Command of the Army of BH, Sefer Halilovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: If you were to analyse this paragraph as an intelligence officer, how would you define Mate Boban's and Alija Izetbegovic's positions? On whose behalf were they signing an agreement?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: This shows that Mate Boban was signing this on behalf of the Croats and Alija Izetbegovic on behalf of the Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Next document, P20 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, this is a document which comes from the accusation, the number -- I mean, it comes from the Office of the Prosecutor, itself. This is an important document, a document from the accusation, a document that we have seen on numerous occasions already. Witness, this document states that there was first, before that, on the 3rd of March, 1993, in New York - you were not there, you could not know - that there was an agreement that was signed between Izetbegovic, Halilovic, Boban, and Akmadzic, and six members, the names of whom were quoted, were to co-ordinate and prepare for something. On the 24th of April, with the presence of the international community, represented by its very best representatives, by the elite, Lord Owen, Ambassador Peter Hall, Mr. Okun, whom we met here. So all of the Croatian elite and the elite from Bosnia-Herzegovina, the ambassador in Zagreb, were present, attended. So a document was signed by the three highest political representatives, Mate Boban, Tudjman, and Izetbegovic. So I see this document -- well, unless I don't understand anything, but I'm reading what I see, and I see that there are two armies, the BH Army and the HVO, that there are conflicts, and so it is requested that these conflicts be ended immediately. It is requested also that there be an agreement about the legality of both armies and about the establishment of a joint command, all this with the agreement of the international community. And Appendix 1 now, which was not presented to you by Ms. Alaburic, but which is appended, Annex 1 shows, and this is written black on white - I'm not making it up, I'm just reading what I see - that the BH Army and the HVO are two separate entities in their command structures, that these two identities are in charge of personnel, logistics, administration, training, morale, and identity matters; that there must be a joint command for an operational control of the military districts, and that this joint command will consist of General Halilovic and General Petkovic, who is here sitting in this courtroom. And, actually, I will also ask him questions when he's on the witness stand. So, Mr. Witness, did you -- at your level at the time, and we're in the month of April, were you aware that there had been an agreement between all of these personalities and that this agreement was about a joint command which was to be made both by Halilovic and Petkovic? Were you aware of that, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right, so you were aware of it. And how did you know about it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, at the time I was with the Main Staff of the HVO. I learned this from the chief of the Military Intelligence Service, who told me that he had been informed about this by General Petkovic. This was said at one of our meetings within the Military Intelligence Service, and everyone present was told about this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. And did you know that this agreement had been endorsed, sponsored, under the aegis of the international community?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, in relation to this agreement, it was something that we knew about, just as we knew about all the other high-level agreements that were reached under the auspices of the international community.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Okay. So this agreement includes a parameter which was not mentioned. The signatories agreed to say that there may have been infringements of rights about the civilian population and that possibly there were crimes which were committed, and that while in order for these crimes to be established, an international commission -- an independent special commission must be established which will define the facts. Did you know that Mr. Izetbegovic, Mr. Boban, Mr. Tudjman, had agreed for such a commission to look into the crimes which may have been perpetrated by the various parties?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I didn't know about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right, so you did not know about that. That's what I wanted to know, because, you know, that refers to part of the document. Okay, Ms. Alaburic, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I would also like to put a question to you with regard to this document. In the first part of it, that is, written in italics and large font, number 3, the second sentence runs like this: "In particular, they," that is, the signatories, "urge military units of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina and of the Croatian Defence Council to immediately start implementing the agreement on the legality of both the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina and the HVO ..." I'm not interested in what comes afterwards. But I would like you to tell me, if you have any view on this, what is meant by implementing the agreement on the legality of these two armies?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, what that means is that the BH Army and the HVO were equally legal and that they were to set up a joint command. Following this -- or, rather, pursuant to this addendum number 1, steps were taken to achieve this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm not interested in the amendment. Thank you for the answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, I do not share this point of view, and I must say something. In the English text, there's the word "and," which clearly connects the question of legality to the command -- to the Joint Command. I mean, it's written here in the English text, and this refers to Annex 1. So Annex 1, from my point of view, and I may be wrong on this - I do not know everything - Annex 1 complements the question about the Joint Command, and the legality seems to be connected to the two armies. So what do you think about this? You're not a legal expert, you may not be able to read an international agreement, but in your mind is there a connection between this Joint Command and these two armies?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, there is a connection. One must establish a joint command for these two armies. They exist as such, and now both are to be placed under a joint command.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, if I may say, this was not interpreted correctly, which has not been a problem so far, but I do have to say it now, or, rather, translate it. In Croatian, this reads "for them to start the implementation of the provisions of this agreement to the effect that the BH Army and the HVO are equally legal." The Croatian text does not state the same thing as interpreted or translated. An agreement on legality, that is not mentioned anywhere. You've all learned enough B/C/S to notice that yourselves, I'm sure. This sentence describes the substance of the agreement. If we look at 2D470, which is the document that we were looking at before, the Petkovic-Halilovic agreement from Zenica reached on the 20th of April, 1993, the agreement has no title, as such. And Article 1 says that the BH Army and the HVO are legal armed forces of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina and that they are to receive the same treatment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Previous translation continues]... testify, so she made a comment, but it would have more weight if it came from you. In your language, could you please read paragraph 3, because when they signed this document, it was almost 1.00 a.m., and I presume that Mr. Tudjman, Mr. Izetbegovic, and Mr. Boban did not know -- or did not know English well, that they have signed the document in their own language, which they read and understand, and that they trusted the translators, the English-speaking translators who were there, who made the text in English, and it's important to point out that it's the Croatian version which is binding. That being said, the three politicians also signed the English text, but it does say that the Croatian text applies. So, of course, you know this language very well, and thanks to the help of our interpreters, we're going to hear the translation. Can you please read paragraph 3 in your language?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Your Honour. "Co-signatories. The co-signatories of this joint statement call on all commanders and units of the BH Army and the HVO to unconditionally comply with all of the agreements so far reached between the representatives of the Croatian and Muslim peoples in the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina." In particular, they call on the military units of the BH Army and the HVO to start implementing, without any further delay, the provisions of the agreement on the fact that the BH Army and the HVO are equally legal units, and on the establishment of a joint command of these forces comprising representatives of both staffs, in parentheses "(Annex 1)."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. I must say that in the French translation I heard, it was very clear, that the fact that the BH Army and the HVO are legal entities. This is absolutely obvious in the interpretation I received from the French booth. Therefore, the ambiguity in the English translation seems to create doubt as to the legality, whereas in the French I received, there is no ambiguity. These two armies are legal, both of them. I believe it was important that you should read this text in your own language so that it could be interpreted by our interpreters, who are extremely experienced and very knowledgeable. Thank you. Ms. Alaburic.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jasak, you were answering questions by Judge Antonetti about this annex, P2091. You said that you heard about the substance of these agreements from your boss, the VOS chief; right?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: During your time with the VOS, did you ever hold briefings or meetings?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, on a regular basis, every day.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Would your chief normally inform you of any information received elsewhere, at other meetings or in a different way, pertaining to anything that the service was in charge of?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: He informed us regularly about everything he believed was required for our work.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Did the VOS chief ever meet the chief of the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: They met on a regular basis and whenever required.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Do you have any information indicating that the chief of the Main Staff sometimes informed the VOS chief of any information that he had obtained at other meetings, or conferences, or something that he had gleaned from reports from the field and that he believed was relevant?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Whatever was pertinent to the work of our service and the work of the Main Staff was exchanged and forwarded. To all practical intents, the VOS chief's office and the chief of the Main Staff's office were two adjacent rooms with a door connecting them.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Where was your room?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: My room was right next to the VOS chief's room, with a connecting door.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: His Honour Judge Antonetti asked you everything about P2091. In view of that, I will only have a brief question. These two armies, the chiefs of staff of these two armies, the commanders agreed that the HVO and the BH Army would keep their own separate identities and commands. Nevertheless, they would be setting up a joint command, too. Based on your information, did the HVO, in fact, continue to function as an independent, separate unit and entity?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, indeed it did.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: We'll be looking at a document now, a document that's been much discussed in this courtroom, 4D1611. This is an order dated the 14th of June, 1993, signed by president of the BH Presidency, Alija Izetbegovic, and addressed to both the BH Army and the HVO. This is on a memorandum of the HVO. Mr. Jasak, can you please try and explain, as long as you know about how the mail circulated about the Main Staff, how this could possibly happen?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: If there was a document that was faxed a number of times and still not completely legible, and then it was faxed through to a new address, so much along the same lines I see that a copy was made here of an order by the Presidency of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, signed by the president of the BH Presidency, Alija Izetbegovic. The only thing missing here that I can notice is a stamp telling us who produced the copy.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Did you know about this BH Presidency order from Geneva at the time it was actually delivered, which was in mid-June 1993?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I knew about it.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Our next document --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, in this Trial Chamber we have discussed this document for hours, and everyone knows this document; Judges, Prosecution, Defence counsel, everyone. Ms. Alaburic asked you for an explanation, and you gave us one, and you seem to say that there must have been an original order by Mr. Izetbegovic which was copied. That's one possibility, but there could be others, including one that I will give you, but it's just a working hypothesis. In Geneva, on June 13th, 1993, June 13th, Mr. Izetbegovic, on behalf of the Presidency, because you see that on item 4 that the Presidency made this decision unanimously and in its full composition, so he is asking for the cessation of hostilities between the two armies. He says that those responsible for this are Delic and Petkovic, and he's also asking the UNPROFOR to provide its services. I would like to know whether, on June 13th in Geneva, Mr. Izetbegovic told everyone that this was this order, that this order would have been maybe sent by telephone or by another media to the HVO Main Staff, because this would explain why an unidentified officer typed this document and, on the next day, i.e., June 14th, after having recorded this document in the log-book, because we have a reference number 02-2/1, and so forth and so on, this document is -- once typed, is sent to all operational zones. So it seems that there could have been a verbal order transmitted or conveyed by who knows whom, and at the staff the entire order is being retyped. Is this a possibility; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I don't know what was agreed in Geneva. I do know about this part, where I assume how this came about. Whenever similar documents arrived that were not entirely legible, they would be retyped, and the only thing that remained was for someone to put a stamp there in order to certify that the copy was identical to the original. The kind of paper used for fax messages fades very soon. I don't know if anything was attached to this to certify that the copy was faithful to the original or not.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Our next document - and then later I'll be asking questions about these BH Presidency decisions - 4D1586. It's a decision by the BH Presidency on a Presidency memorandum. The date is the 20th of July, 1993, signed by President Alija Izetbegovic. Paragraph 1, just as in the previous document, the units of the BH Army and of the HVO are called upon to immediately and unconditionally cease any mutual attacks.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: What I want to know about, Mr. Jasak, is this fact that the BH Presidency is here seen to be issuing orders that apply both to the HVO and to the BH Army. To begin with, let's look at the handwritten portion, which reads: "For Keza." Can you explain what that means?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can. "Keza" is Zarko Keza. He's the VOS chief, Zarko Keza. The signature here belongs to Nikola Mikulic, who was an official of the VOS as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell us, do these signatures mean that this document arrived in the VOS?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they do.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: If we look at the upper part of this document, we can see that the document was sent from the Ministry of Foreign Affairs of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Does this follow from the number?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And it says here "Ministry of Foreign Affairs," but I can't see the number. It might be by satellite telephone. I can't tell what this is about by the number, but you can see where it came from.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: To the best of your knowledge, did VOS have information to the effect that the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina was also issuing commands to the Croatian Defence Council?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: VOS had to know this, because it says here, For the chief, and quite a few documents used to arrive in VOS by fax because the fax machine worked better than the other equipment we had.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: The next document is 4D --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, there is a preamble to this decision, explaining why the decision was actually made, and I note that the province of Sarajevo, there was a session of the Presidency held on July 19, 1993, and during this session they agreed to adopt the three items in this decision. This is what is written. Given this, from Sarajevo on July 20th, maybe by fax, maybe, we're not sure, but it probably is because on the top of the document we have the wording from Ministry of Foreign Affairs, BH, phone number -- with a phone number, and this must have been sent to the staff, which means that between Sarajevo and the staff there was communication. When it arrived, your chief and your colleague, Nikolic -- Keza and Nikolic both wrote on this document to prove that they had obtained the document. Now, if this is what happened, could you tell us to whom your chief sent this document? This is July 20th. Mr. Petkovic is still chief of the Main Staff. According to you, what did Keza and Nikolic do with this document, or maybe yourself? Who did they send it to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, it's not "Nikolic," but "Mikulic," Nikola Mikulic, who signed this for Keza. We can see that at the bottom. I can't tell whose handwriting this is, but it may have arrived in VOS from the chief of the Main Staff or it might have been forwarded by VOS to the chief of the Main Staff. Regardless of the fax number it arrived at, the chief of the Main Staff and the chief of the VOS certainly both knew about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have a technical question. I believe that it should have been put to you ages ago, and I apologise for not having thought about it earlier. To your knowledge, could you tell us whether there was a telephone connection or a fax connection between Sarajevo and this building where you were located?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the building where we were, there was a telefax which could be used to communicate with any place that had a telephone, because we had a secure line, and any country in the world, wherever there was a telephone or a fax, messages could be sent.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're saying that the entire world could communicate with you by fax, because there's a number. And I saw a document where we had the telephone numbers and the fax numbers. We could take a look at it, if need be. So you do confirm that it was possible to receive documents from anywhere, and since they had communication devices, the Presidency probably sent this text?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell us, Mr. Jasak, as regards the possibility of communicating with Sarajevo - that's what His Honour was getting at - of course you could communicate with the whole world, but the question is: Could you communicate with Sarajevo throughout all this time by phone or fax directly?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was possible to communicate with Sarajevo if the telephone lines in Sarajevo were in order, if they were working. If there was fighting and in the fighting telephone lines were destroyed, then it would not be possible.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jasak, I'm asking you about facts. Do you know whether the lines were working the whole time, and did communication with Sarajevo take place?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no information that communications with Sarajevo took place. I was speaking hypothetically. We could communicate with the whole world. It was an assumption of mine.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Well, it's clear to us, hypothetically, if there are lines, one can communicate. The question is: Do you have any information about the actual facts? Was it really possible to communicate with Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: These are among the first such documents I have seen. I had no knowledge that such documents arrived prior to these.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: All right. Let's continue with our topic. The next document dealing with the HVO as an integral part of the armed forces is 4D1234. You don't need to look. You can listen to me reading it. This is a draft of the Washington Agreement, and in item 6 the military agreement is defined. Where were you, Mr. Jasak, in March 1994?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: In March 1994, I was in Zagreb, in the Staff Command School.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Did you know at the time that the Washington Agreement was being signed between the Croatian and Muslim sides in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: After the signing of this agreement, were the HVO and the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina -- or, rather, did they continue to function as separate entities with their own commands?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they did.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Among the people close to you, was someone appointed the commander of the Main Staff of the HVO?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not among the people I was close to, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Well, maybe I misunderstood you, then. Who was appointed chief of the Main Staff after Tihomir Blaskic?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: After Tihomir Blaskic, Zivko Budimir was appointed.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Did you know Mr. Budimir personally?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: I was referring to him. I do apologise if you weren't close friends, so I confused you by saying that. I apologise. The last document dealing with this topic, 4D826, the Law on Defence of the Federation of Bosnia-Herzegovina. The law was enacted by the Constitutional Assembly of the Federation of Bosnia-Herzegovina at a session held on the 9th of July, 1996. In Article 37, item 2, it says that the army of the federation consists of the units of the BH Army and the HVO. To the best of your knowledge, what were the component parts, in reality, of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The HVO and the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Did you have colleagues who were in the HVO and then continued working in the army of the federation?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Do you have any knowledge as to whether the time they spent in the HVO was recognised in their years of service?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do have such knowledge, and, yes, the time they spent in the HVO was credited to them for their years of service.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Did these soldiers and officers who came from the HVO have the same rights as the soldiers and officers of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina or was there a distinction between them?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: They had absolutely the same rights. There was no difference whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Jasak, we'll now go back to topics concerning combat in the period from 1992 to 1993. You told us that the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina and the HVO co-operated in the course of 1992, if you recall, when we were talking about the time of the war in Bosnia-Herzegovina; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Let's look at 4D1700, 4D1700. This is a command for defence of the Central Bosnia Operations Zone. The document was created in March 1996 [as interpreted], as confirmed by General Filipovic, who participated in the drafting of this order. Please help us to understand this order. Tell us, Mr. Jasak, in view of your military experience and training, do you know what the structure of a defence order should be?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell us, what is defined first in such an order?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: In every order, the first thing to be defined is the enemy, and that's done by the VOS.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Let's look at this order issued by Tihomir Blaskic. In item 1, in the introductory part of this order, is the enemy defined?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Who is the enemy, according to this order?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to this order, the enemy is the VRS or, rather, the units listed here by number.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: In item 2 of this order, subparagraph 3, neighbours are defined; to the right, parts of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Tell us, Mr. Jasak, when you define a neighbour in this way, are you referring to an ally or an enemy?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: We are referring to an ally.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: In the order, in item 5.1, the task is defined, and it says that it should be carried out in joint action with the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. And the same is stated in item 5.3. Mr. Jasak, please tell us, what does it mean when you carry out a combat task in joint action with another army?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It means to co-ordinate the activities of two units, because the best possibility of breaking through the line is where the two units -- or, rather, the line is most vulnerable at the point where two units meet if their action is not co-ordinated.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: If you, as an intelligence officer, had to explain, based on this document, who was the HVO's enemy in Central Bosnia at this point of time, what would you say?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would say that the only enemy was the VRS.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Let's look at the next document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: May I ask a question probably of you, Ms. Alaburic. On page 62, line 2 and 3, you are here reported as saying that the document was created in March 1996, and that strikes me as rather improbable.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, thank you for your intervention. I regret we didn't spot the error. I said "in 1993," in 1993. Yes, we have noted this down as something to be corrected, but it's better like this. In the Croatian language, there was no doubt that we are talking about 1993.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Let's look at the next document, 4D475. This is an order for active defence, dated the 23rd of February, 1993. It was issued by Miljenko Lasic, the commander of the South-Eastern Herzegovina Zone -- Operative Zone. In item 1, we have information about the enemy. Who is defined as the enemy here, Mr. Jasak?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The VRS is defined as the enemy, the 4th Herzegovina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: In --

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Excuse me. Not the 4th, just the Herzegovina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: In item 2 of this order, it says that part of the units of the 4th Corps of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina has been assigned some tasks. Can you comment on this?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Please do.

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The units carrying out defence are defined here, including the Stjepan Radic HVO Brigade, the 1st HVO Brigade, Knez Domagoj, the 3rd HVO Brigade, the 2nd HVO Brigade, and this is not really legible, the Herceg Stjepan Brigade, part of the units of the 4th Corps of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, the Cannon/Rocket Regiment, tank battalion and home defence units, home guard units, and then the task is defined: To organise defence line at current positions. On the right side at Cavaska Gomila.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jasak, there's no need for you to read us the document. Could you just comment on it, please, from the viewpoint of co-operation and the relations between the HVO and the BH Army?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The HVO units and the BH Army units here are jointly taking part in defence against the VRS.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: In item 3, the 4th Corps of the BH Army is defined as "the neighbour," so let's recall how this is to be interpreted. Is a neighbour a friend or an enemy?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: A neighbour is a friend.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: In item 5.3, we can see that some tasks are assigned to the Bregava Brigade of the BH Army and, in 5.5, to the 1st Mostar Brigade. And another piece of information, and then we'll summarise this. We can see that this order was also sent to the 4th Corps of the BH Army. Mr. Jasak, can you comment on the fact that a confidential piece of information, such as this order for defence, was sent to the 4th Corps of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can. This order was sent to all those participating in active defence. This includes two units, the Bregava Brigade and the 1st Mostar Brigade, who are participating in the defence, and they were part of the 4th Corps. So together with the HVO, they were opposing the VRS. This sort of document may be forwarded only to the greatest of friends because, on the contrary, if such a document were to fall into enemy hands, it would threaten the entire combat disposition.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Colonel, earlier you said that it was forwarded to the neighbours, so to a friend. I'm not quite convinced about that. Sometimes, well, you have neighbours with whom you're not necessarily very friendly. Now, I see this document for the first time, I must say, and I have noted, without you saying it, that it was forwarded to the 4th Corps, so Mr. Pasalic has knowledge of these elements. So I see in this document some information which usually armies keep as top-secret information; number of fighters, means, assets, et cetera. And here the "army," [as interpreted] quote/unquote --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Sorry, the interpreter apologises, "the enemy."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- is communicated information which can be used between Pasalic and the HVO, so he's given information, and the person giving the information is Mr. Lasic in person. When it says that given unit has this and that sort of weapons, this or that assets, it means that you actually give information -- military information. For instance, the Motorised Brigade -- the Bileca Motorised Brigade, it says that there are 1400 fighters in this brigade, and that it is reinforced with tanks, with two howitzers, 120-millimetres, and so on and so on. So Mr. Pasalic is given information. So you, as an expert of military intelligence of the time, when you give information of that nature to a military entity which is another entity, do you give that rather to an enemy or to a friend?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, information is provided to friends exclusively. The brigade you mentioned here, the Bileca Motorised Brigade, was an enemy unit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Right. Well, when I said that, I was wondering about it. And so it's a BH Army brigade, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour. That was a brigade of the VRS.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fair enough. So when you give this information to the 4th Corps, and this is information which were received from the forces -- about the forces of Republika Srpska, it means that you do not hide anything; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, there was no concealment. Nothing was being hidden. Information about the enemy was provided and about our own forces.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now, I'm a Judge, and in my modest capacity I'm trying to understand, and I do not make any headway. We are in February, on the 23rd of February exactly. And as we can see, there are connections between the HVO and the BH Army. But we know that before that, that were problems in January, in October, in Prozor. We know that there were conflicts. So how do you connect those past conflicts, present or future conflicts, with such a document? I mean, what sort of explanation do you have? What does it mean in reality?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, this means, in reality, that the only enemy both of the HVO and of the BH Army was the VRS, and the conflicts on the ground -- well, within 24 hours everything was done to obtain a truce.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jasak, His Honour Judge Antonetti is entirely right when he claims that you also had a neighbour with whom you were not entertaining friendly relations. For that reason, I would now like to ask you to define for us the term "neighbour" as it occurs in these military documents, so not generally speaking but in military terms. When, in a military document, we come across the term "neighbour," what exactly does that mean?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: If we define someone as a neighbour, it means this: Each unit has a left neighbour and a right neighbour. These neighbours must be friendly. At all points where two units link up, there has to be the closest possible co-operation in order to prevent the front-line from being penetrated by the enemy.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: All right. Let us assume we have a unit in a certain area. Right next to this area is an area controlled by the enemy. How, then, will you define this line between your own unit and the territory that is under the control of the enemy?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The enemy is the enemy. No special marking needs to be done. It's just a line. If we have a defending unit, then there are neighbours both to the left and to the right involved in the same defence effort as neighbouring units; friendly ones, at any rate.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: May I therefore conclude, and correct me if I'm wrong, you face an area that is under the control of the enemy, in a colloquial sense you are neighbours, in terms of being adjacent; nevertheless, this enemy unit would fall under the heading "Enemy" and not be defined as a neighbour?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In military terminology, as far as I know, only a friendly unit can be defined as a neighbour. Everyone else falls under the definition of an enemy.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: The only thing separating you from the enemy is the front-line; right?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: All right. Mr. Jasak, we've just seen two orders in relation to two operations zones, and we saw what the relationship was like towards the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Based on your knowledge, did the HVO perhaps have any contingency plans for combat operations for the purposes of which the BH Army was defined as an enemy?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The HVO had no contingency plans for the purposes of which the BH Army was defined as an enemy.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jasak, to the best of your knowledge as a resident of Mostar, an official of the Main Staff, a person who was directly in touch with soldiers and military commanders, do you know anything about the HVO preparing for clashes with the BH Army?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no knowledge of that at all.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Given the English interpretation, it means you know nothing about that, or do you mean the HVO was not preparing for clashes with the BH Army?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The HVO was not preparing for any clashes with the BH Army.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: The next document is 4D1355. This is an interview given by General Milivoj Petkovic in mid-1994 on the eve of his departure from Herceg-Bosna. Question number 5 and question number 6 from the end of the document, we see the journalist asking the following question: "The result in the war against the Muslims were somewhat poor?" And the general's reply was: "That's right." The next question: "Were they not the weaker enemy?" And the general's reply: "No, they were not. The distribution of the Croatian population is such that we form enclaves all over the place. The distribution of power was unfavorable, and we had not been preparing to fight them. Everyone took their own decisions at a local level, and everyone assumed nothing would happen over here because our relations are good." Mr. Jasak, given your personal experience and given your knowledge, which I referred to in the introductory part of my previous question, the facts stated in this particular reply by General Petkovic are correct, aren't they?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my opinion, these facts are absolutely correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us whether the military commanders and the authorities of Herceg-Bosna were surprised by what happened in mid-April 1993? Without for the time being going into such questions as to who attacked whom, were they not surprised by the sheer volume of the fighting and combat on the part of the BH Army? Were they surprised and were they ready to face anything like that.

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were certainly entirely surprised. The sheer force of the attack that occurred and the units involved were such that they could have been better used to lift the blockade of Sarajevo, had they decided to use the same amount of force for that purpose.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jasak, do you know anything about how General Petkovic, in his capacity as the chief of the Main Staff, wanted to go about resolving various incidents, innocent misunderstandings, even clashes between the BH Army and the HVO?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Petkovic did his best to resolve each and every conflict by negotiating and by peaceful means and methods.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Were you to say what General Petkovic focused on in particular during your time with the Main Staff, what could you tell us?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I could say that for the most part, he focused on negotiations of all different kinds, under the auspices of the international community or without its presence, meaning negotiating directly with BH Army representatives.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Did you at any point hear that anyone at the Main Staff, or in any of the bodies that you were in touch with, criticised General Petkovic for spending too much time on international negotiations, saying that he was too peaceable, too peace-loving, and that the Main Staff should be run in a different way?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: One could overhear remarks to the effect that the general should be more energetic, more vigorous, and not give way as much as he used to.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Let's look at the section of this interview where the general is asked a very similar question about whether he really should have tried to put a stop to each and every conflict. It's the third question from the end of the interview. General Petkovic says: "Some say we could have scored a success immediately over there. Perhaps we could have in Mostar, too. When liberating Mostar, they had nothing apart from a poorly armed, independent battalion. Nevertheless, who at the time would even have considered a conflict with the Muslims? Our own brigades had Muslim members, after all. The clashes around Prozor were what they were. There weren't any civilian casualties. The clashes around Vakuf were stopped from Geneva." General Petkovic says here: "Who could have imagined any clashes with the Muslims at the time?" Sir, as long as your familiarity with General Petkovic allows you to answer the question, please go ahead and answer it. If not, please just say so. The question is this: Could General Petkovic have uttered this sentence, honestly believing that back then nobody had even been able to imagine that the HVO would at some time clash with the Muslims?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can honestly confirm that this sentence means what it says, and it is entirely consistent with General Petkovic's actions on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: The next sentence: "Our own brigades, after all, comprise Muslim soldiers." My conclusion would be that General Petkovic considered the presence of those Muslims in the HVO units to be a factor potentially preventing any clashes between the BH Army and the HVO. Mr. Jasak, in view of your acquaintance with General Petkovic, in view of your opinion regarding General Petkovic, did he, indeed, believe these Muslims in the HVO to be a factor of stability, potentially preventing any clashes with the Muslims, since "we had Muslims within our own ranks," that being the general reasoning?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. General Petkovic saw these Muslims as a bridge, a link, if you like, between the BH Army and the HVO. He also honestly believed that this fact alone would stop any clashes from erupting, or at least any serious ones. If there were to be any clashes, they would be minor ones that could easily be put out within a 24-hour period.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I realise it's time for a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, we're going to take a break. I only have a small question, a very quick one, about this document. It's an interesting document, this interview of General Petkovic, and I will certainly have the opportunity with him to talk about this document in light of what is included in the interview, but a point of detail that you may be able to confirm or not. At some point, he's asked about the staff and the fact that on two occasions he was head of staff, and General Petkovic explains that with General Praljak there was an agreement to break down the tasks in two areas, Central Bosnia and Rama-Uskoplje. From your standpoint, from your position, did you learn that, in fact, there was no one head of staff, but two, and that they had split among themselves the territory and the competencies relating to those territories?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I was not aware of there being two chiefs or two commanders. At one point in time, I don't know exactly what it was called, a chief of staff or the staff commander, and I think it was roughly the same time that General Petkovic mentions. At any rate, General Petkovic spent quite some time negotiating in Central Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. So you don't have any specific knowledge about this. Let's take a 20-minute break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The court is back in session. Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. It's a very short request, Your Honour. Our response to the objections by the Prosecution to our IC list in relation to the witness Maric is due first thing tomorrow morning. We ask, and the Prosecution have no objection to this, I can tell Your Honours, that we ask that in the light of the scheduling, may we have until Thursday to do that? We're sitting tomorrow morning, as Your Honours appreciate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. The Trial Chamber is granting you leave for that. Ms. Alaburic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President. If we could while Mr. Stewart is on his feet, or at least after he's been on his feet, make a similar request. I think we also owe -- my apologies. I believe we may owe two responses as well, and I'm not sure we can get them filed by tomorrow. So as I mentioned to Mr. Stewart when he came across, if we could have a similar extension until Thursday, that would be appreciated as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Well, for equality of arms, of course we grant you leave also. Ms. Alaburic, you have two hours and fifty-nine minutes left.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right, Your Honours. More on this subject that is related to General Petkovic personally, very briefly. 4D397 is our next document. This is a letter written by General Petkovic in June 1992 and addressed to the Municipal Staffs of the HVO in Konjic and Gornji Vakuf because of tensions and incidents involving the Territorial Defence. The letter states: "I hope you didn't forget that the TO and the HVO are integral parts of the Armed Forces of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Instead of strengthening their mutual bonds in the fight against our common enemy, standing at the very threshold of your municipality, you are preparing to use weapons against each other. In the name of both Croats and Muslims, I beg you to overcome this situation. As members of the Armed Forces of Bosnia-Herzegovina, you are obliged to do that."

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jasak, regardless of the fact that the document bears no title, do you consider this document to be an order or a simple request?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is quite clear that the document is a mere request, or a recommendation, if you like, telling them how they should join forces against their common enemy, and the enemy's already standing, as it were, at the threshold of their home.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Did you know General Petkovic back then in June of 1992?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I knew him, but not as well as I did later on. I knew that he was the chief or the commander.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: I won't be asking you any personal questions, then. 4D433, that is our next document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, I have a short follow-up question. We have here a personal document written by Mr. Petkovic and dated June 20th, 1992, telling the Konjic municipality that they're not supposed to forget the TO and HVO are integral parts of the Armed Forces of Bosnia and Herzegovina. This is a statement made by Mr. Petkovic to a political entity. It's a top-secret message, and it's also encoded. Mr. Petkovic is expressing something in this message and is very clear. Now, I would like to know whether this was shared by all HVO soldiers in June 1992.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, there is no way I can know what all the other soldiers believed. I can tell you what I believed, and I believed this, and this belief was shared by those I actually knew.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jasak, given the fact that sometimes the distinction between the civilian HVO and the military HVO is unclear based on documents, tell us this: If this was dispatched to the Municipal Staff of the HVO, would that be a civilian body or a military body?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The staff was a military body.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: And what was the name of the civilian HVO in Donji Vakuf -- Gornji Vakuf?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know exactly what it was called. Probably "the HVO," no more than that. At the time, municipal staffs comprised the military.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jasak, if I may be allowed to ask a leading question that is of no particular significance but that might be useful, if I try to look at the signature, and then based on that try and understand whether this was the civilian component or the military component of the HVO, could we say that a document would be signed by a commander on behalf of the military component of the HVO and the president on behalf of the civilian component of the HVO?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that would be understood. I have no doubt that this is a military document. It was signed by the commander, and it's addressed to the Municipal Staff. Therefore, it was understood that on the 26th this would be forwarded to the military commands or the municipal staffs.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: 4D433, instructions by the chief of the Main Staff, Milivoj Petkovic, sent to the Konjic Main Staff, to be delivered to Sagolj personally. The date is the 20th of January, 1993. It's about allaying tensions in Konjic. It reads: "Establish contact with the BH Army in Konjic and make an effort to allay any tensions." Mr. Jasak, by this time you are with the Main Staff already and you are personally acquainted with General Petkovic. If we look at these instructions, is this something that he can be said to have considered an appropriate way of dealing with any problems with the BH Army?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: These instructions, this note, reflect very faithfully General Petkovic's modus operandi.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: You're trying to say that this is exactly what Petkovic did, himself; right?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell us, if you can, in relation to individual municipalities, was the situation in a given municipality in any relation whatsoever to the ability of the municipal commander to establish and maintain good relations with his counterpart in the BH Army?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: By all means, the ability to negotiate was a very important factor. When you have armed men on both sides, it's very easy to soon have incidents occurring or clashes erupting, unless everybody tries to use their common sense.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: I have a particular question about the operations zone that you were analysing, Mr. Jasak. The 23rd of March, 1993, does that date have any special significance for you?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 23rd of March; is that what you asked?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Yes, precisely.

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was when the clashes erupted in Konjic municipality.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Did you in the VOS have any information about those clashes?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we did.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Based on such information as you had, who attacked whom?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to our information, it was the BH Army units that attacked the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Look at the next document, 4D125. This is an order dated the 23rd of March, 1993, co-signed by Milivoj Petkovic, on behalf of the HVO, and Arif Pasalic, on behalf of the 4th Corps of the BH Army, and this is an order to stop all fighting between the HVO and the BH Army. Mr. Jasak, in the VOS did you have information showing that the conflicts were stopped, based on this order on the same day --

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we did.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: -- in Konjic?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: The next two documents I have prepared --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, I was looking at this document jointly signed by Pasalic and Petkovic, and I was quite interested to note that this document is headed with the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina and the HVO, Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna. Now, Pasalic is a BH Army officer, but he is signing a document coming from the HVO, on HVO letterhead. Of course, Pasalic cannot tell us why he actually signed this document, since he passed away. But you are a military intelligence specialist, so could you give us an explanation? Could you answer us why the top man in the BH Army in the Mostar area would sign a document on HVO letterhead? Because it's not a neutral document. It is on HVO letterhead. How can you explain this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, if we look at the document, underneath the coat of arms of Herceg-Bosna, it says "Main Staff of the HVO," and to the right it says "4th Corps Command," and this document with the HVO heading, in my view, is the way it is because both sides wanted to halt the conflict quickly. It was drawn up based on an agreement between General Petkovic and Mr. Arif Pasalic in the HVO Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Earlier, you said that the BH Army started attacking the HVO as of March 23, 1993. But if on the same day Pasalic signs a document asking for -- according to which there is an order for a cease-fire, why is it that there's still an attack? How can you reconcile this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, there were several instances whereas such cease-fires were signed, but not respected. The conflicts continued. Either it was impossible to keep the troops on the ground under control, or the negotiations on the part of the BH Army were not entered into sincerely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So who's responsible for the situation, according to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that the leadership of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina is responsible.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: The next two documents, Mr. Jasak, you can just listen. P3805 is an UNPROFOR document. Let me just check whether it's under seal. It doesn't seem to be. And from this document, it transpires that on the 30th of July, 1993, an agreement on cessation of all hostilities was signed at Sarajevo Airport by the representatives of the three warring sides in Bosnia-Herzegovina, and on behalf of the Croatian side it was signed by Milivoj Petkovic. Based on this agreement, Milivoj Petkovic issued an order on cessation of hostilities. That's P3816. These were activities that took place in 1993. Do you know when General Praljak came to the head of the Main Staff of the HVO?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was on the 23rd of July, or thereabouts, in 1993, but I don't know whether this is the period when the HVO had both a commander and a chief of the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Very well. We'll see that from the documents we'll see shortly. But what I want to know now is the following: Do you know who dealt with issues of co-operation with UNPROFOR and participating in international conferences at the time when General Praljak was the first man in the HVO Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Petkovic continued dealing with these matters.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: I will now ask you to look at P --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, please tell me if I'm wrong. If I'm wrong, tell me, you know. I won't take offence; of course not. I'm trying to understand, and we have thousands and thousands of documents to look at and it's very difficult to know exactly what happened. Now, we have a document from the international community, and I believe that it shouldn't be contested. Well, you never know. Well, the international community is mentioning the agreement, and Mr. Mladic is mentioned also, the notorious Mladic still at large, and we all hope that sometime he will come to be tried. Anyway, Mr. Mladic is speaking and is talking about the situation of 3.000 Croats who fled from Bugojno towards the Serbian lines. I'm sure you know that there had been a BH Army offensive in Bugojno which led to the Croats fleeing the area. But here we find out that the Croats left for the Serbian lines, which probably means that the Serbs were not shooting at them, and that General Mladic is trying to solve the situation through this document, so maybe through exchange of prisoners, or maybe he believes that these Croats are prisoners. We don't really know exactly what he wants to do. But I always believed, you know, that in order to understand the conflict, you don't just have to say that it's a conflict between Muslims and Croats, but you have to integrate the Serbian component into this in order to understand what exactly unfolded. Now, do you believe that I'm wrong in trying to do so or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, throughout the war the VRS was defined as the enemy. In part, for one year, the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina was an enemy of the HVO.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You haven't really answered my question. I understand what you said, but this is what I'm trying to ascertain: If I interpret all the events that unfolded only looking from the angle of what happened between Croats and Muslims, don't you think I would be making a mistake if I forget to include the Serbian component?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I don't fully understand your question. Do you mean to say that the Serbs had an influence on the conflict between the Croats and the Muslims?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. To a certain extent, I would say, Yes. I would like to know the following: When looking at the situation on the ground, what happened on the ground, the fact that the BH Army attacked in Bugojno, for example, the fact that 3.000 Croats flee towards the Serb lines, not in another direction, I would like to know whether there's an explanation for this. When there is this conflict between the Muslims and Croats, don't you think we should --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction, "do you think."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- that we should also take into account the Serbian component? Are we supposed to consider the conflict only from the angle of Croats against Muslims?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, when the Croats came under attack, they ran every which way, so it's quite possible, because if they fled in one direction, they would be sure to be in danger of their lives, and they weren't sure what would happen if they ran the other way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're saying that the enemy was the Serbs, but we have 3.000 Croats fleeing towards the Serbian lines. Why is that? Were they told that nothing would happen to them? Were there agreements that we don't know about? Everything is very strange.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I don't know of any agreement, but they knew that if they fled in one direction, they would be killed immediately. If they fled in the other direction, they might stay alive somehow. And there was no way they could flee in a third direction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I understand you.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's try to analyse this more broadly.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: If you had to explain to Their Honours something that's important for the understanding of the war in Bosnia-Herzegovina, would you have to include the Serbian side in your explanation? Would you have to explain that there were also Serbs there, that they had their own authorities, their own army, what their aims were, what their relations with the Muslim army and the HVO were? Are the Serbs a relevant factor for Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: As regards the Serbs, they also come from the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina, but there is a difference. When there was a referendum for the independence of Bosnia-Herzegovina, the Croats and the Muslims voted for independence and the Serbs did not, but they certainly have the right to their own space within Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: If you wish to understand the events in Bosnia-Herzegovina, or in some parts of Bosnia-Herzegovina, do you have to know something about what the Serbs are doing and what they want?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes. The Serbs want to create their own ethnic territory. They want their own area.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: So you have to know something about the activities of the Serbs in order to understand the situation in Bosnia-Herzegovina? That was the gist of Judge Antonetti's question.

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, quite simply, I didn't understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Very well. Tell us, if we wanted to explain to Their Honours how it came about that the Croats were in an enclave in the Konjic municipality, the villages of Turija, Zaslivlje, and Zabrdje, and managed to survive there, would we have to tell Their Honours something about the Serbs as well?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the Croats there managed to survive because at the local level they established contacts with the Serbs, and that's how they managed to survive.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: And now an example that His Honour used, Bugojno. It's outside the operations zone we are discussing, but the principle is the same.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness repeat the answer, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: For the full understanding -- [In English] I surrender.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: The interpreters have asked for the witness to repeat the answer. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] To understand the situation, when a specific question was asked which I understood, for example, the Croatian enclave of Turija, Zabrdje, and Zaslivlje managed to survive thanks to the Serbs because they managed to reach an agreement at the local level. It is also possible that something like that happened on the territory of Bugojno.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: And now the question asked by Judge Antonetti was the following: For the full understanding of the events on the ground, for example, the events in Bugojno, do we have to know something about the activities of the Serbian side; were they co-operating with someone, were they letting civilians pass through, were they supplying someone with weapons, and so on?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Well, tell us, why do we have to know that?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, because - and I'm now referring to the area of Turija, Zabrdje, and Zaslivlje - it was only by co-operation that the lives of those people could be saved.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jasak, I'm not asking you why the Croats co-operated with the Serbs in some areas. I am asking you why we have to know something about the activities and plans of the Serbs in order to understand the situation on the ground.

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I don't understand your question.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: The question is: What do we have to know in order to understand properly the situation on the ground? If on the ground you have three armies, three civilian authorities, the question is: Is it enough to know only about what the Muslims and the Croats are doing, or do you have to know what the Serbs are doing and thinking, if possible?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, you have to know about the activities of all three sides.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Witness, can you explain to the Chamber how you have a general view and a knowledge of the problems the Chamber has to deal with that you can give such an answer? I think it's not a proper question, but how can you tell us -- how can you give us such an answer? Do you know what problems the Chamber has to deal with, what is important, what is not?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Mr. President, Judge Trechsel, I believe that remark or comment or question was improper, and I'll say why. We have been struggling for the last four years, or nearly four years, to put matters into context. The question of why, obviously, goes for context. Now, we're not dealing with the situation in Iraq, Afghanistan, Switzerland, Hungary, France, or wherever. We're dealing with a situation when none of us were there. You were some place else. Some of us may have been in the region and may think we know what was happening because we were working in certain positions or reading the newspapers, but now we have an individual who was there, and we need to put things in context. Now, I understand that some members of the Trial Bench believe that everything is tu quoque, and we're concerned about that, that everything was done by the Croats against the Muslims, they were the aggressors, there's only one army, and the perception that some of us are getting is we shouldn't even have a trial because, you know, certain minds have already been made up. That's a perception. We're trying to change what we believe is a perception, hopefully not a reality. Now, this gentleman, if he was in the army and if he was there, if he was associated with the general, obviously he would be in a position to know why it is necessary for someone to understand the situation, be it a judge, be it a prosecutor, be it an individual, his neighbour, why it's necessary to know what is happening on the ground and what all three sides are doing. I think that is important. Now, a more relevant question is whether the individual knows. Does he have any personal knowledge upon which he can answer that question? But I don't think that you can possible -- you can possibly begin to fathom and understand what is happening if you're saying, We don't want to hear about the one side. And this is why I'm extremely troubled when, for instance, you -- in our particular case, you have chosen deliberately to exclude official gazettes of other municipalities when we're trying to show what they're doing, not for tu quoque, but to show there are limitations upon which all -- everybody was working under, because it seems to us that if you are isolating everything and you're just looking at one piece of evidence in isolation, it is easy to get to the wrong conclusion. I certainly believe the gentleman can give us an opinion as to why he believes it is necessary for everyone, not just the Judges, for everyone to know what all three sides are doing. Whether he is -- whether you want to give any weight to that answer, that's another question. Now, maybe a predicate needs to be asked. Can the gentleman -- is he in a position to give such information? If so, what gives -- on what basis does he -- you know, does he have this information, more details. But I do believe, Your Honour, with the deepest respects, that the manner in which you address the witness and suggesting that he doesn't know anything and shouldn't be commenting, I think, is improper.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Mr. Karnavas, I must really reject this criticism of one and a half pages, almost, of a question. If you believe that the Chamber, after three and three-quarters of years of hearing this case, needs this witness, who was a medium-level officer, to tell the Chamber what is relevant to decide this case, I think it is not a proper question. The Chamber knows what's relevant. That's not the issue, Mr. Karnavas. I'm not -- I have not in any way suggested that this was not something that could be of some interest, but I think it is really not a question this witness, having in mind of what we have heard from him so far, is the person to answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, Judge Trechsel, I believe, then, the objection should have been to the counsel, not to the witness. The witness was asked the question. He was merely trying to answer a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: That's more or less what I did. I said I thought this was not a proper question for this witness, Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, I apologise if in any way I've offended the Bench, but it seemed to me that perhaps if a counsel asked the wrong question, counsel should be admonished or corrected. The gentleman, in my opinion, was merely trying to give an answer. Now, perhaps he doesn't have the proper foundation or the proper foundation wasn't laid. Perhaps with more foundational questions, he would be in a position to answer that question. But this gentleman doesn't know what we know or what has happened in the last three and a half years.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I have, in fact, asked what his foundation was, Mr. Karnavas. It may have slipped your mind because you were all worked up already, filled with a sort of paranoic fear that the Chamber had all sorts of ideas that you suppose and bring up again and again. But I think we can close it here. Okay?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, I do know Your Honour wishes to close it, but I do wish to go and say something on behalf of the Petkovic Defence, and it's one of those happy occasions where I spoke what Mr. Karnavas has said. I'm in a mildly more awkward position, because so far as it might be said that what Your Honour said to the witness ought to be deflected to counsel, then, of course, it's my lead counsel, but my lead counsel is easily tough enough to deal with any such points that might be raised by one of the learned Judges in relation to her, and I have every confidence in her to deal directly with any point that's put fairly and squarely to her. But, Your Honour, it was -- and Mr. Karnavas is right. It was, with respect, not fair to put the point to the witness in the way that you did, to be asking a witness, Do you know what problems the Chamber has to deal with, what is important, what is not. Mr. Karnavas is right. The witness just answered the question, and not only did he just answer the question, but as it happens, a question directed to a witness in relation to understanding the situation on the ground goes right to what Mr. Karnavas was saying was -- the witness was there, he was on the ground. This is not purely opinion he's being asked. It's not expert evidence he's being asked. He's being asked to convey what he actually saw and what he experienced and what he knows from being there at the time. And, really, it goes back to -- there's been a lot of stuff about foundation, but if a witness is going to do that, it's entirely fair to ask him, then, whether, based on his knowledge of his being there at the time, whether it -- in fact, to convey that knowledge and to give the Trial Chamber the facts as he sees them, which is his job as a witness, it is enough to know only about what the Muslims and the Croats were doing or did you have to know what the Serbs were doing. He was a soldier, and anybody in these armies -- it's ridiculous to suppose that anybody at his level in the army doesn't have a knowledge and a grasp of what you needed to know and what you needed to understand about what that third party was doing at the time. That must have been part of the -- well, I suppose I'm speculating a bit, but the day-to-day conversation amongst soldiers. Your Honour, it wasn't fair to the witness, with respect, and Mr. Karnavas was right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I object to the interference, that my question and my ideas are ridiculous, Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour needs to read carefully what I said, but I'm entitled to make my submissions in firm forensic terms and I -- well, it's there on the transcript, Your Honour. We can all read it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, well, actually, I'm the origin of the problem, the source of the problem, because I asked a question from the document, and maybe that's where your misunderstanding comes from. I thought I asked a question which was clear. You said, I don't understand the questions. Ms. Alaburic rephrased the question in better terms, and you still told her, I do not understand the question. So I should have told you, sir, we have a document coming from the headquarters of Kiseljak, and this is a document sent by Mr. Victor Andrew to a Cedric Thornberry in charge of civil affairs. This is a document which has two aspects: one a political aspect and one military aspect. The political aspect is about the discussions in Geneva, and the military issue is that this document states that there is an agreement between three people, Mladic, Delic and Petkovic, who are three high-level commanders, military commanders.
